title: Jason Arday: Cambridge professor in plagiarism row quits
description: The University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row has resigned "with immediate effect". Prof Jason Arday said he had "concluded
body: The University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row has resigned "with immediate effect". Prof Jason Arday said he had "concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away". Earlier, the university said it had launched an investigation "following new information" about Arday's "academic qualifications and honorary appointments". It comes after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in Arday's work and questioned some of his stated achievements. The academic has admitted errors in his work, but has insisted he is not "a liar".In a statement posted by the Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said that being appointed professor had been "without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life". "The years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack," he said, adding "there comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great". He said his resignation should not "be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge. "Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me." Thanking his students and colleagues, he said that "for my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away".Arday said "this is not the end of my work" and that he needed "time to heal". "When that time comes, I will return," he added. Earlier on Wednesday, the university said its inquiry had begun "following new information" about Arday's "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".It added that there remained "a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct".In its statement, the University of Cambridge said: "While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law."We also fully recognise that there is a person at the centre of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him." Jesus College, where Arday is a fellow, has said it is launching its own process "parallel" to the university's investigation.In 2023, the then 37-year-old sociologist became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge.Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".He claimed on Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".On Saturday, Arday told the Times in an interview that he was accountable for those mistakes, but that "what I am not is a liar".He told the newspaper: "There has been, since I arrived at Cambridge, a very well orchestrated and co-ordinated campaign to unseat me from my position."He suggested that this was "racially motivated" and that he had become a "lightning rod" for criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policy.Arday said some errors in his early academic work was because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information, and that similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics."We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the newspaper.

schema.headline: Jason Arday: Cambridge professor in plagiarism row quits

title: Disney agrees deal to let TikTokers use its characters in videos
description: Disney and TikTok have agreed a deal which will allow creators to use clips from Disney films, including its subsidiaries, in their videos.It means cl
body: Disney and TikTok have agreed a deal which will allow creators to use clips from Disney films, including its subsidiaries, in their videos.It means clips from hit franchises like Star Wars, Toy Story and the Marvel Cinematic Universe will soon start popping up in videos - which will also be shared on Disney's short-form video platform, Verts.The scheme will be launched in the US before being rolled out to other countries.Neither company shared financial details of the agreement, although it follows the collapse of a $1bn (£745m) deal between Disney and OpenAI which would have let people use its characters in AI-generated videos.That agreement was cancelled in March when OpenAI shut down its AI video generation tool Sora, citing a decision to focus on other parts of its business."Today, fans are celebrating our stories in entirely new ways," said Disney's chief marketing and brand officer Asad Ayaz, following the TikTok deal being announced."Disney owns some of the world's biggest franchises but ownership of attention is shifting towards creators," social media expert Matt Navarra told BBC News."Hollywood used to market at fans - now it needs to give fans the raw materials to market with it, and that is quite a profound shift."TikTok said its platform saw an average of 6.5 million posts relating to film and TV per day last year.Fans like to use clips from films and TV shows in their videos, but without express permission, they would often be taken down due to copyright claims.This makes it harder for a wide audience to engage with fan-created content around a big release.TikTok would also benefit from the "credibility of becoming a formal distribution partner to one of Hollywood's biggest studios," Navarra said.He added that TikTok's recommendation algorithm gives it the power to "influence which character or scene or forgotten franchise suddenly becomes very valuable again".Disney and TikTok said a jointly-run programme would boost some creators' videos and give them access to exclusive events."This is a deal that repositions and recovers Disney in the UGC [user-generated content] space following the content gap left by the sudden collapse of Sora," Gareth Sutcliffe from Enders Analysis said. But he said it was not without risk."There is an ongoing safety debate around TikTok under European online rules," he said."At a minimum, Disney will need to employ significant guardrails to curate the creator content that is selected."Online creators and influencers are becoming more important to brands' marketing strategies.Last year, a report from Oxford Economics said YouTube content creators contributed £2.2bn to the UK economy in 2024 and supported 45,000 jobs.There is also a recognition that even very small influencers, who focus on niche topics, might have lower follower counts but come with a hyper-engaged audience.Disney launched its short form video platform Verts in the US in March, with plans to expand that further around the world.

schema.headline: Disney agrees deal to let TikTokers use its characters in videos

title: After deadly Kyiv strike, Ukraine warns interceptor shortage is costing lives
description: At the Kvitneva railway station near Kyiv, workers lift white body bags from the pockmarked platform and carry them to waiting ambulances. Shoes, glas
body: At the Kvitneva railway station near Kyiv, workers lift white body bags from the pockmarked platform and carry them to waiting ambulances. Shoes, glasses and some pieces of clothing mark the spot where eight people were killed during Russia's latest massive aerial attack on Ukraine. Overnight, Moscow fired 115 drones and 24 ballistic missiles. Most of the drones were shot down, but Kyiv's depleted air defences did not intercept any of the missiles. Twenty-one people were killed and dozens more were injured.The latest Russian barrage destroyed storage and logistics facilities - from online retailer warehouses to a postal sorting centre. In Kvitneva, it is not clear if the target was the railway itself or the warehouse beside it, which was also hit and was still smouldering hours later. Down the road, another warehouse was still ablaze more than 12 hours after the attack. The attack started just after midnight, with very little warning. It was one of the most intense nights of bombardment Kyiv has endured in recent months.Nearby, Anastasiia Dudley's house was almost totally destroyed but she and her mother survived – shaken but unharmed.Anastasiia has lived through years of war - but Wednesday was her "scariest night" since the start of Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022, she says.She looks up at the precariously leaning walls of her house, which she says was hit by a drone a few hours before missiles struck the warehouse and the station nearby."You see two floors - the first and the second, but it was a three-floor house with a roof," she says. The building's top floor has been sliced off. "So no roof, no third floor, and extensive damage on the second floor. It's pretty unstable".Ukrainians have lived through four-and-a-half years of war, but now air defences are increasingly vulnerable, resulting in dozens of deaths at a time. For years, Ukraine has relied on US supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.But the US has used many of its stockpiles during its war with Iran and is reluctant to give up more. After initially offering Ukraine the license to make Patriots in early July, last week President Donald Trump denied the US had agreed to "give away that kind of technology".Yet without them, Ukraine's skies are wide open."Ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today," President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Last week, following another deadly attack in which only one out of 27 missiles was shot down, he warned that a shortage of interceptors "encourages Russia to launch such attacks that take human lives".On Wednesday again Zelensky made a direct link between the delays in supply and the "horrific casualties and destruction" witnessed regularly across Ukraine. "Quite literally every single day, the lives of people here in Ukraine depend on the decisiveness of our partners in Europe and America," he said later, adding he had spoken to Nato chief Mark Rutte about getting interceptor missiles.Ukraine has an undisclosed number of Patriot systems, but it is the Patriot interceptor missiles which are in short supply.It takes at least two to bring down each incoming ballistic missile and the system has a range of around 160km (99m), so effectively placing units can be difficult. Russia, meanwhile, uses on average between 20 and 30 ballistic missiles each time it carries out large-scale strikes on Ukraine. Ukrainian military expert and former intelligence service officer Ivan Stupak says the lack of interceptors left Kyiv in a situation comparable to having a supercar in the garage but no petrol."Imagine you own a Lamborghini but have no fuel," he tells the BBC. "You have one of the best cars in the world, but you can't drive anywhere... The situation with Patriot is similar. The systems are there, but there are no interceptor missiles."A lack of Patriot missiles leaves the whole country exposed – including the valuable Patriot systems."Now the question is how to protect the systems themselves from being destroyed," Stupak says. "Because they could very well become priority targets for the Russian Federation."Until we receive more interceptor missiles, these systems need to be relocated or concealed somehow so the Russians cannot detect and destroy them. Right now they're extremely vulnerable."At the railway station as the medics leave the scene, another team moves in quickly to repair the power lines above the track so services can resume. This is the rapid recovery and clear-up Ukrainians have become all too familiar with.But they know their skies can still light up with deadly force at a moment's notice. Countering that threat and keeping people here safe can depend on decisions about production and distribution of interceptors made many miles from Ukraine's borders.

schema.headline: After deadly Kyiv strike, Ukraine warns interceptor shortage is costing lives

title: Newcastle appoint Matthias Jaissle: What will new manager bring to club?
description: Matthias Jaissle has quite an act to follow at Newcastle United."It won't be easy to succeed Eddie [Howe]," a source said.Just like Newcastle's moves
body: Matthias Jaissle has quite an act to follow at Newcastle United."It won't be easy to succeed Eddie [Howe]," a source said.Just like Newcastle's moves to sign young players from the continent, there is an element of risk with this appointment as the club bring in a manager who has never coached in the Premier League before.German Jaissle delivered success in Saudi Arabia and Austria - with Al-Ahli and Red Bull Salzburg respectively - but this will be the first time he has sampled life in one of Europe's top five leagues.He becomes the Premier League's second-youngest current head coach, at 38, and his first competitive game is against Liverpool on Sunday, 23 August.In the statement announcing his appointment on Wednesday, Jaissle said it was an "incredible honour" to become head coach of "one of the biggest clubs in European football"."My teams are built on togetherness, hard work, intensity and a passion to improve every single day," he added."I believe there is enormous potential within this squad and throughout the football club. "I give my complete commitment and total energy to bringing further success to Newcastle United."There has been no time to waste since Jaissle arrived at Newcastle's pre-season training camp in Spain at the weekend."He will try to understand the culture, what Newcastle means to the community, as soon as possible," added a source."That's what he will live by."Howe certainly set the standard.The Englishman took charge of a side in relegation trouble, kept them up, then went on to end Newcastle's long wait for silverware by winning the EFL Cup in 2025 - and also qualified for the Champions League on multiple occasions.However, last season was a bruising one domestically - Newcastle finished in 12th place - and Howe watched Alexander Isak, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon leave within a year.Newcastle are set to lose a fourth key player too, with captain Bruno Guimaraes heading to Arsenal.They need a progressive manager to start a new cycle following Howe's decision to step down - and build on what he did at the peak of his reign.Effectively, Jaissle's remit will be to develop players and outperform clubs with bigger wage bills. And Newcastle's squad should expect him to be just as demanding as his predecessor in training."We did lots of small-sided games to keep the intensity high and if someone had not been giving it their all, he called them out on it," said former Salzburg midfielder Zlatko Junuzovic."He's not afraid to address things head-on."Jaissle has quickly had to get to know a new set of players, but he will encounter a group who are already used to similar principles from their time under Howe, as well as new young signings who are eager to learn.He also brings with him a group of coaches and analysts who will look to quickly get his message across.Al-Ahli defender Merih Demiral knows that better than most."Looking forward to going to training every day was so important," he added. "They paid great attention to every detail and always made sure we were fully prepared."Matthias has built a really strong team around him and they played a huge role in our success."Jaissle and his staff will be working with a squad whose average age has dropped significantly this summer.However, the German will still rely on experienced heads such as Dan Burn and Fabian Schar in the dressing room.Jaissle, a former defender with Hoffenheim, was a few months younger than Junuzovic when he took charge of Salzburg in 2021.But he did not shirk in telling the midfielder he would find it difficult playing alongside the younger players in the side.Jaissle challenged Junuzovic to improve and earn his place in the starting line-up, and "kept his word" when he did."He understands the players' language," the former Austria international said.It is a little telling that Red Bull Salzburg have not won the league since Jaissle departed following his second successive triumph three years ago.The Austrian club have not reached the Champions League knockout stage, either, since doing so for the first time ever under Jaissle in 2022, even if they were ultimately hammered 8-1 on aggregate by Bayern Munich in the last 16.Jaissle went on to show an ability to adapt at Al-Ahli with a different profile of player, winning back-to-back Asian Champions League titles.As much as his aggressive side pressed high, and got the ball forward quickly, they also had solid defensive foundations and no other team conceded fewer goals in the Saudi Pro League last season. Such a balanced approach will be needed if Jaissle is to succeed in the Premier League, which is a different beast altogether, as he will soon find out.But Newcastle's new boss will certainly back himself."The best way to describe him is his mentality," said Turkey international Demiral. "Even if we were losing 2-0 or 3-0, he never lost his belief. He always believed in his players and prepared us with the same mindset in training."This is one of the main reasons why we managed to come back and win so many matches."It's a very different league, and challenge, but Newcastle will hope it's a sign of things to come.Jaissle's predecessor Howe had similar principles in terms of building a side around physical intensity, pressing and direct attacks.The German primarily uses a high-pressing 4-4-2 when the opposition are building from the back. Even when his teams are pushed into more of a mid-block, they have shown an impressive understanding of when to step forward and transition into a high press as a collective. Howe's defensive tactics should align well with the Red Bull style of pressing, which could make it easier for the players to buy into Jaissle's methods.What Howe was criticised for towards the end of his tenure was a supposed lack of adaptability.After joining Al-Ahli, Jaissle inherited a mosaic of superstars and less experienced Saudi players - a wildly different challenge from coaching a Red Bull club with consistency and understanding in style from youth level through to the first team.While he retained his coaching principles, he recognised the need to platform players according to their individual strengths within that framework.The Premier League is constantly evolving, with coaches designing new counter-measures to tactics that appear to work from one week to the next.If Jaissle is going to succeed in the Premier League, that agility will be a vital asset.

schema.headline: Newcastle appoint Matthias Jaissle: What will new manager bring to club?

title: Italy waste workers help winner find €1m lottery ticket
description: A lottery player who accidentally binned a €1m (£857,158) winning-ticket may be the luckiest person in Italy after refuse workers found the missing sl
body: A lottery player who accidentally binned a €1m (£857,158) winning-ticket may be the luckiest person in Italy after refuse workers found the missing slip.The anonymous player disposed of the ticket in a shop in Bitonto, southern Italy, after checking their numbers and being told it was "non-payable".The person only realised they threw away a winning ticket after a relative pointed out the numbers they always played had been drawn. It sparked a two-day search through a "mountain of waste" which had been collected by a bin lorry, the head of the refuse company, Roberto Nicola Toscano, told Italian news agency Ansa. "This story is nothing short of miraculous," he added.Recounting the story, he said the mix-up happened because the "non-payable" message appears when the prize is too high to be paid out by the shop. When the player returned home, their family reportedly pointed out their favourite numbers - 2, 4, 8, 10, and 51 - had been drawn. "It was then that they realised the misunderstanding. So they all went to the shop together and discovered that the tickets had been thrown away and collected by one of our operators," said Toscano, director of SANB who handles waste collection in the area.After the player made contact with the refuse company, the bin lorry was located before its contents were compacted for disposal. "Luckily it was a Sunday, otherwise the load would have already ended up in landfill," the boss told Italian broadcaster TGCOM24. The truck was then escorted to a special site where the search began to find the "small piece of paper hidden in a mountain of waste". Finally after a two-day search, the winning ticket was reportedly found by a waste worker on Tuesday morning, with the workers cheering as if they had won the prize themselves. "It was in a hole-ridden bag along with other damaged tickets: this was one of the few intact ones," Toscano told Ansa. The cost of the recovery operation is set to be charged to the winner, who had previously signed a declaration promising to cover the search costs. Toscano told BBC News that he was not authorised to reveal any details on the identity of the winner.But the luck rubbed off - when Toscano and his colleagues bought a scratch card as a joke, they won €50 (£43).

schema.headline: Italy waste workers help winner find €1m lottery ticket

title: Family 'devastated' by death of girl, 9, as man charged with murder
description: Image source, Police ScotlandImage caption, Minnie Merriman was described by her family as "incredible, beautiful and brave"ByGraeme OgstonBBC Tayside
body: Image source, Police ScotlandImage caption, Minnie Merriman was described by her family as "incredible, beautiful and brave"ByGraeme OgstonBBC Tayside and Central reporterUpdated 6 hours agoThe family of a nine-year-old girl who died after being found seriously injured in Arbroath have said they are "devastated" at her loss, as a man appeared in court charged with her murder.Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, died in Dundee's Ninewells Hospital on Monday. A 35-year-old man, who police said was known to the girl, has appeared in court charged with her murder.Christopher Rice from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, made no plea during an appearance in private at Forfar Sheriff Court and was remanded in custody.Image caption, Christopher Rice was remanded in custody following an appearance at Forfar Sheriff CourtHe is expected to appear again in court next week.Officers were called to the Elliot Industrial Estate in Arbroath shortly after midnight on Monday following reports that a child had been found injured.In a statement issued through Police Scotland, Minnie's family said: "We are devastated with the loss of our beloved, absolutely incredible, beautiful and brave Minnie Moo. "Our family asks that our privacy is respected at this extremely difficult time."Image caption, A Minnie Mouse toy was among the tributes left at the scene of the incident in ArbroathPolice said they are not looking for anyone else in connection with her death and the other members of the family - who were camping in the area - are being supported by specialist officers.Det Insp Mike Ness said: "Our thoughts remain with everyone affected by these events, especially Minnie's family."A police presence will remain in the area while our inquiries continue.""Anyone with any concerns, or information, should approach these officers or contact Police Scotland., externalImage caption, Police were called to reports of a child being injured while camping in Arbroath

schema.headline: Family 'devastated' by death of girl, 9, as man charged with murder

title: SpaceX: What can scientists learn from a Falcon 9 rocket hitting the Moon?
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The last time it was confirmed that part of a rocket had collided with the Moon by accident was in 2022ByPallab Gh
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The last time it was confirmed that part of a rocket had collided with the Moon by accident was in 2022ByPallab GhoshScience CorrespondentA stray SpaceX rocket is believed to have crashed into the Moon, forming a crater near a famous lunar landmark and giving scientists a unique research opportunity that could help future missions.The empty upper stage of a Falcon 9 rocket was due to strike the Moon near the Einstein crater at a speed of about 5,400mph (8,700km/h) on Wednesday.The short, dramatic flash it created would have been hard to catch by amateur astronomers even with high-end telescopes, but larger observatories in the Americas are analysing the information.It could be days or even weeks before the full picture of what happened and what we can learn from it is known - but for planetary geologists, this accidental collision is a scientific gift.Figure caption, Watch: Science Museum's head of space on what scientists will look for after crashSpace X's Falcon 9 rocket is a reusable model and has been sent into space on several missions. Its design allows part of the rocket to return to Earth, but other sections are shed in space.The rocket blasted off from Florida in January last year, carrying two lunar landers into space.Its job was to fire the upper stage hard enough to send both of the landers out of Earth's orbit and onto a path towards the Moon - mission accomplished.The spent stage - which is about the size of a five-storey building and weighs at least 4,000kg - was left drifting in a long, looping orbit that swung out towards the Moon and back again. Over the next 18 months, the gentle gravitational tug of the Earth, Moon and Sun, along with even light from the Sun, gave a faint push. Astronomers tracking the rocket part eventually worked out that those small nudges had put it on a course towards the Moon and was picking up speed every day.The impact at around 07:35 BST (06:35 GMT) on Wednesday happened in broad daylight for many parts of the world, but the tiny flash it produced would have been far too faint to see, even through a telescope. Amateur astronomers observing in darkness would also have had little realistic chance of seeing the flash, given that it would have lasted a fraction of a second and occured on a part of the Moon bathed in daylight. And so it may also have been hard for them to see a plume of dust stretching as far as 100km (62 miles) that lasted for several minutes.Even spacecraft orbiting the Moon were not in the right place at the right time to watch the impact happen live. South Korea's Danuri orbiter had the best chance, having passed near the crash site shortly beforehand. Its team has told Korean media that any footage will only be released once researchers have completed their analysis.Over the next few days, Nasa's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter will be in position to photograph the site, allowing images before and after the crash to be compared.Image source, NASAImage caption, The Einstein crater is over 180km (112 miles) wide, and is large enough to contain a smaller crater insideThe science and probably the first images might come from powerful telescopes in the Americas where the sky was still dark. Even then, turning the detection of a 14m object hitting a daylight part of the  lunar surface i385,000km away won't be easy but not impossible.Image processing to clean up the picture can take hours, days or even weeks, as scientists check and process the data.But the sight of the new crater from the orbiting spacecraft will be eagerly anticipated. Because researchers already know the rocket's exact size, speed and point of impact, this collision turns from being a random accident into a rare, controlled experiment. It is a dream moment for planetary scientists because it lets them test their models of how impacts dig out craters, throw debris across the surface, and send tremors through the Moon's interior.That has real practical value. Understanding how much rock and dust an impact throws up will help engineers design safer landers and future Moon bases, working out how far flying debris can travel and how hard the ground might shake nearby.Material thrown up from beneath the surface offers fresh clues about the Moon's geology, adding to what scientists already know about how the Earth-Moon system formed some 4.5 billion years ago.This is not the first time a human-made object has struck the Moon. Since 1959, dozens of spacecraft have crashed into it, some by accident and many deliberately for science. The Soviet probe Luna 2 was the first, followed over the decades by Nasa's Ranger probes in the 1960s, several Apollo-era rocket stages, and more recently the LCROSS mission in 2009, which was deliberately crashed to search for water ice.The last confirmed accidental impact, in 2022, was thought to be the leftover booster from a Chinese lunar mission launched back in 2014 - a reminder that this sort of space debris has been quietly piling up above our heads for well over half a century.Figure caption, The space junk clean-up!

schema.headline: SpaceX: What can scientists learn from a Falcon 9 rocket hitting the Moon?

title: Police chief considers legal action over PC Harper killers' early release
description: The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and is not eligible for early release. Speaking on the Today programme, Thames Vall
body: The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and is not eligible for early release. Speaking on the Today programme, Thames Valley Police chief Jason Hogg urged the government to reconsider its position.Only prisoners convicted of murder, rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme in England and Wales - while those convicted of manslaughter remain eligible."I fully understand the challenges around the crisis in the prison system," he said. "But the decision made and where that line has been drawn, I do not believe that people responsible for taking the life of another citizen in our country should be released early." He said: "I was informed yesterday that the Police Federation are considering legal action, I am in discussions with the Police Federation with regards to this matter".Asked whether this meant he would join them, he said: "I think we need to get some legal advice in relation to this. This is something I certainly would consider."Following PC Harper's death and a campaign by his widow Lissie, Parliament passed "Harper's Law", which gives mandatory life sentences to the killers of emergency services workers. It also doubles the maximum penalty from 12 months to two years for those who assault police or other emergency workers. But the new rules - introduced in 2022 - did not apply retrospectively to the sentencing of PC Harper's killers, and so do not prevent them from being released early. Hogg said: "The law isn't retrospective and we all understand that, but the fact that they are released early simply seems perverse."Aileen O'Connor, branch chairman of Thames Valley Police Federation told BBC Breakfast her organisation was exploring whether legal action was an option."If it is an avenue we can explore then I'll get behind that 110%," she said.As for what shape a potential legal challenge might take, she said: "Ultimately that's for the specialists, the barristers and those in that legal sector to make that decision whether there is a challenge there."If there is a challenge then we will look to take that challenge."Sentencing minister Jake Richards told the BBC it would be wrong to pick out individual cases and block two of PC Harper's killers from early release.Although the government had reviewed what sentences would be excluded from the early release scheme, he confirmed "manslaughter is not one of those offences". On Wednesday the Ministry of Justice released a new list of exclusions that will be exempt from the early release scheme. It said rapists, as well as criminals sentenced for child sex offences and grooming and conspiracy offences for these crimes, will no longer be eligible to leave prison early.Murderers and terrorists were already not eligible for the early release scheme.Richards said: "It would be wrong to pick out individual cases within different offending cohorts. That wouldn't be right. It wouldn't be lawful either. So it is correct that those two individuals will be subject to the new regime from October".Any legal challenge would have to be heard in the High Court, where ministerial decisions are reviewed.Judges would have to be convinced that the government's choice of who gets out and who remains inside was either totally unlawful because they did not have the power to decide - or so irrational that it failed a legal test for reasonable decision-making. Crucially, judges do not rule against a minister just because they do not like the choice they have made - there has to be a clear legal flaw in how they went about it.Met Police commissioner Mark Rowley said the PC Harper case has had "a chilling effect on the confidence of police officers when they see a justice system that's not prepared to support their bravery".On Tuesday Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the government wanted to go further but warned that a prison capacity crisis would be likely if fewer prisoners were allowed early release.Norris apologised to families who would be affected by the early release scheme and stressed that the government wanted to go further "but we cannot". "We have to make this decision, we've been able to make some changes to it, but we have to have the rest of the sentencing act changes otherwise we run out of prison places in November and that can't happen," he said.The justice secretary said 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October.Approximately 1,000 prisoners will now not be released early following the revision to the scheme, he clarified.The government also announced an extra £10m will go to front-line victim support services, including a new national helpline.Additional reporting by home and legal correspondent Dominic Casciani

schema.headline: Police chief considers legal action over PC Harper killers' early release

title: Sonam Wangchuk: Protests weakened Narendra Modi, activist tells BBC after hunger strike
description: The recent youth-led protests have weakened Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi "terribly", says leading activist Sonam Wangchuk whose hunger strike g
body: The recent youth-led protests have weakened Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi "terribly", says leading activist Sonam Wangchuk whose hunger strike galvanised the movement.Wangchuk told the BBC that the atmosphere in the country had changed following  mass demonstrations which triggered the resignation of the education minister on 25 July.Young people now have more confidence they can "change things if they want to" and feel they don't have to "take everything lying down", the 59-year-old said.The "cockroach" movement mounted one of the biggest public displays of dissent against Modi's government, which has been in power since 2014.The movement takes its name from a remark by India's chief justice, who drew criticism after comparing sections of unemployed young people to "cockroaches" during a court hearing.Wangchuk fasted in scorching heat in the capital, Delhi, for 26 days in June and July, consuming only salt and water. He says he has now regained six of the 11kg he lost. The activist was forcibly taken to hospitals which he says were "more like prisons" for the final six days of his fast.By then, the protests had escalated from public anger about the leak of exam papers into some of the biggest anti-government demonstrations India had seen in years.Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned the day after Wangchuk ended his hunger strike.Since then, Modi has announced fast-track courts to try those accused in the leaks and appointed a tech billionaire to lead efforts to reform the examination system.The government also said it would offer compensation to families of students who took their own lives after exam questions were leaked.But India's problems are deeper - with graduate unemployment hovering around 35-40% for the past 25 years.Wangchuk argues fundamental reform to education is needed.The engineer and education specialist says exams currently have little relevance to the job market.Often based on multiple-choice questions, they are designed to assess millions of students efficiently, with no consideration of how effectively they measure skills and understanding, he says. This, in turn, shapes how schools teach.If exams placed greater emphasis on hands-on experience and aptitude, he suggests, schools might adapt their methods and help address India's jobs crisis."There needs to be some planning of what the world and the country are likely to look like in 15 years," Wangchuk says.Changing the way children are taught might help ensure they are "not left unemployed and sectors that need people are not left underemployed". India's government has previously defended itself against criticism of its handling of the economy. It argues that claims of an unemployment crisis are overstated and that its macroeconomic policy remains fundamentally robust.Wangchuk insists change is in the air in India.He believes the government has been hugely damaged by how long it took before Pradhan stepped down."This gave young people a chance to gain confidence and unity in their actions."Wangchuk says that, if the government doesn't listen to the people, they may return to protests that go beyond education.He suggests the damage is already being felt by the governing BJP, pointing to the party losing two of three by-elections this week - including a seat in Bihar state it had held for more than 30 years.However, he maintains that India's leaders could still change their approach."I always believe in people realising their mistakes and amending their ways. So I would give them that chance."Twelve days have now passed since Wangchuk said he broke his fast. He is back in Leh, his hometown in the Himalayan region of Ladakh.He has a renewed faith in the power of hunger strikes - taking inspiration from Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of non-violent resistance.In previous years he's held hunger strikes for more self-rule in Ladakh and against a "very powerful government" seeking to "bulldoze ecologically sensitive places".Though he has not achieved his goals there, he says "inflicting pain on ourselves makes the government feel differently, compared to us using sticks and stones". Asked if he has any plans to run for office, he says no - he would rather enable others to do so.

schema.headline: Sonam Wangchuk: Protests weakened Narendra Modi, activist tells BBC after hunger strike

title: Woman arrested after four stabbed in central London
description: Figure caption, Moment woman is arrested in Covent GardenByJames W KellyLondonNisha PatelReporting fromreporting from Covent Garden and Amy ClarkeUpda
body: Figure caption, Moment woman is arrested in Covent GardenByJames W KellyLondonNisha PatelReporting fromreporting from Covent Garden and Amy ClarkeUpdated 4 hours agoA 47-year-old woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden in central London, the Metropolitan Police said.The men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were taken to hospital after emergency services were called to reports of a stabbing in Endell Street at about 12:30 BST. The force said two men remain in hospital with injuries not thought to be life threatening or life changing while the other two have been discharged.The woman was arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault. The Met said it was believed to have been a mental health-related incident. Ch Supt Jason Stewart said: "Officers responded within minutes of this incident after receiving a number of reports."While still at an early stage of the investigation, we would like to reassure the community that we currently believe this to be an isolated, mental-health related incident."He added a "visible police presence" would remain in the area while evidence was gathered.Figure caption, Watch: The London Air Ambulance was part of the emergency response but all victims were taken to hospital by roadCrowds looked on as London Air Ambulance landed in nearby Trafalgar Square as part of the emergency service response but the victims were all transported to hospital by road. A cordon that started at High Holborn and covered the St Mungo's homeless centre on the street has now been removed. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A police cordon was taken down after 15:00A spokesperson for St Mungo's said they "could not confirm whether anyone from St Mungo's is involved at this stage"."Our thoughts are with everyone who has been affected by this distressing incident."We are working closely with emergency services on site," they added.Officers had been seen speaking to people before they entered the centre.Image caption, Arjan Gjorga, who manages a fish and chip shop nearby, said he saw the woman being arrestedArjan Gjorga, who manages a fish and chip shop on Endell Street, said a woman had "started stabbing random people".The 48-year-old added: "We saw this lady after a few minutes being arrested – the police responded immediately."Another witness, who did not want to be named, said they saw the stabbings take place outside the Shaftesbury Theatre before the woman made her way down Endell Street.The witness, who wanted to remain anonymous, said: "We noticed she stabbed three people with scissors by the theatre then she came down here and the police were here."An employee at a nearby barber shop said they helped one of the victims call the police after they had been stabbed.The worker, who wished to remain anonymous, said: "One of the victims ran into the shop to call the police."He was traumatised, he was panicked but the police turned up very quickly."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Charli XCX on lying, Love Island and life post-Brat
description: "Was that the truth, or was it a lie?"This is the question posed by Radio 1's Jack Saunders to Charli XCX about an answer she gave in their last inter
body: "Was that the truth, or was it a lie?"This is the question posed by Radio 1's Jack Saunders to Charli XCX about an answer she gave in their last interview. The Apple singer previously told the presenter that she hadn't started making any new music - when in fact she was putting the finishing touches to her new album, Music, Fashion, Film. "Yeah, it was a lie," says Charli. "I'd finished the record pretty much," she tells Saunders during a special performance at the BBC's Maida Vale studios."So I was just lying to your face basically."I knew when I said yes to Reading and Leeds it was going to be about this next album." But why do artists feel they need to keep their plans under wraps, and is there pressure to do so?Released in July, Music, Fashion, Film follow's Charli XCX's huge hit album, Brat. The record became a cultural phenomenon, used in Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign and even resulted in Collins English Dictionary updating its definition of Brat.So why keep her much anticipated follow-up quiet?Publicist Josh Moss tells BBC Newsbeat that at the early stages of a campaign, artists won't be giving much away. "What people don't realise is that there's so much planning and strategy that goes into an album roll out," says Moss, who has represented artists like Maisie Peters, Bruno Mars and SOMBR. "At a time where attention spans have shortened, artists want to sustain excitement pre and post release. "One of the best ways to do that is through drip-feeding information."So is it all just harmless fun, or is this a case of artists being more cautious?Maria Veronese runs media training company Mediapro and says Charli XCX's method may not be a surprise to her fans."She's fun, she's Brat and it's what we expect of her really," says Veronese. "It's what her fan base loves her for."She says a lot of people who use media training, do so because they're nervous about saying things they don't want to. "We just help them go through all of those scenarios. "Talk about bridging techniques, and what they can say instead of things they don't want to say, so we're not telling them to lie."During her interview with Jack Saunders, Charli XCX also discussed the process of getting the album cover together for Music, Fashion, Film.It contains a black-and-white photo of Velvet Underground musician John Cale, fashion heavyweight Marc Jacobs, and film director Martin Scorsese."I will say it was an absolute nightmare," says the singer. "We were really down to the day before that deadline and you know, they're busy guys," she says. "I felt it was one of those moments where I was like this is a once in a lifetime moment, this is probably never going to happen again. "It was really sweet and overwhelming."And she wanted this album to feel like something new and different. "The way that Music, Fashion, Film sounds was like a very sort of deliberate response to the way that Brat sounds. "They're sort of polar opposites."

schema.headline: Charli XCX on lying, Love Island and life post-Brat

title: Drone carrying explosives found at Leipzig airport in Germany
description: A drone carrying an explosive device has been found at a German airport, police say.A robot was deployed at Leipzig/Halle Airport after the device was
body: A drone carrying an explosive device has been found at a German airport, police say.A robot was deployed at Leipzig/Halle Airport after the device was spotted by an employee near Ukrainian cargo planes overnight, according to Saxony police. A second unidentified object also collided with a cargo aircraft near the same airport. It landed in Hanover with minor damage.Germany's interior minister said the incidents showed a "new level of threat". German airports are on high alert following several unauthorised drone flights in recent months over military bases, airports, energy terminals, seaports and logistics companies. Police have warned of a potential Russian involvement which Moscow has denied. Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carry most of the country's aerial cargo.It is also a major hub for the logistics group, DHL.A police spokesman told the BBC that the explosive-laden object had been spotted close to parked Antonov planes.The detonator was removed from the explosive device. Police later carried out a controlled explosion. Flights on the northern runway resumed at 01:55 (23:55 GMT on Tuesday). The southern runway remains closed."All of this does not point to an amateurish approach. We are talking about a professional, hybrid threat scenario that we will continue to address," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said.He did not name any suspects, but suggested the investigation may point to a possible "competition" that "may also involve foreign powers". Ukraine's Ambassador to Germany Oleksii Makeiev told Welt TV: "Who else could it be but Russia?"Russia has not commented.Similar incidents with suspicious drones in Germany have only happened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Peter R Neumann, a professor of Security Studies at King's College London, said on X."Since last night, the drone war has reached Germany. And it exposes a weakness that we've known about for years," he said.In July 2024 a parcel burst into flames on the ground at Leipzig/Halle Airport before it could be loaded onto a DHL cargo plane, one of a series of parcel fires that targeted the UK and EU countries. There are suspicions it could have been sabotage linked to Moscow.The parcels had contained explosive devices that were set off by electronic timers hidden in vibrating massage pillows, according to authorities.Russia has denied any involvement in those incidents.Last year a Chinese woman was convicted  for passing on information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig/Halle Airport to a man spying for Beijing.

schema.headline: Drone carrying explosives found at Leipzig airport in Germany

title: Ex-leader Hasina gambles with vow to return to Bangladesh
description: Former Bangladeshi prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return to her country in December, despite facing the death penalty there for crimes agai
body: Former Bangladeshi prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return to her country in December, despite facing the death penalty there for crimes against humanity.Hasina, who denies the charges, was tried in absentia after fleeing to India during an anti-government uprising in 2024.On the second anniversary of being ousted, Hasina said in an audio broadcast to a crowded press club in Delhi that she "had to go back", but wouldn't announce her exact plans or dates yet.Her Awami League party has been falling apart and Indian officials have been facing pressure to extradite her after a special tribunal in Dhaka sentenced her to death last year for ordering lethal force to be used on protesters.Hasina's virtual meeting with reporters at the Foreign Correspondents' Club in Delhi was her first meeting with the media since she was toppled after 15 years in power.She delivered a speech over an audio link and then took a handful of questions. "I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she said.In the address she alleged that several organisations had turned the 2024 student protests into a "violent movement", without providing any evidence.She has always rejected the charges on which she was convicted as politically motivated. But UN investigators found evidence that she and her government tried to cling to power using systematic, deadly violence.In audio of one phone call verified by BBC Eye, Hasina was heard authorising the deadly crackdown on demonstrators. Prosecutors used the recording as crucial evidence in convicting her. The UN estimates up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the protests, which started as a student-led movement against quotas in government jobs and turned into a mass uprising.The 78-year-old fled Dhaka as tens of thousands of demonstrators held protests and stormed government buildings, including her official residence, plunging the country of more than 170 million into crisis.Soon after she was toppled, an interim government took charge. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party came to power after elections in February this year, with its leader Tarique Rahman now prime minister. His government had already warned local mediase not to publish or broadcast Hasina's comments. After her address, it said it was "outraged" India had allowed her to take part in a public meeting with the media."Our people have firmly resolved that our nation will never again go back to the dark days of fascism and that Bangladesh will never be a client state," a foreign ministry statement said. Hasina's presence in Delhi has strained relations with Bangladesh, which wants her extradited, a request India says it's examining.A return by Hasina to Dhaka, if it happens, is likely to have repercussions, including political unrest."It's a huge risk for her personally. If she does go back to Bangladesh, she will immediately be arrested," says David Bergman, an analyst based in Dhaka.It's likely that supporters of the ruling BNP, as well as the party of the students, the National Citizens Party, Islamists and others could hold rallies demanding that her sentence be carried out.But the stakes are also high for the Awami League, if she does not return.The activities of the party were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.Awami League leaders allege that hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces. Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted."If Ms Hasina doesn't go back, the violence will continue and they will exterminate the Awami League," Mohammad Ali Arafat, a former minister in Ms Hasina's cabinet, who is also overseas, told the BBC.There has been growing discontent among a section of her party that many top leaders had fled the country while leaving mid-level leaders and supporters vulnerable to attacks."It must be to do with the recognition that if Ms Hasina is going to have any relevance to Bangladesh politics in the future, she's got to go back to Bangladesh and face it," David Bergman says.

schema.headline: Ex-leader Hasina gambles with vow to return to Bangladesh

title: From flip flops to fisherman's sandals: How to look after your feet this summer
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterUpdated 9 hours agoFlip-flops have always been a popular solution to sweaty, uncomfortable fe
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterUpdated 9 hours agoFlip-flops have always been a popular solution to sweaty, uncomfortable feet in scorching weather  - and now they've had a revamp. The most stylish way to wear them this summer is with a kitten heel, according to fashion expert and trend forecaster Angela Baidoo."It's not a high heel and it's really kind of easy to just slip in and slip out of," she says.However, heel or not, the flip-flop has earned itself a bad rap for lack of support and damaging our feet. Is that fair? Why your summer shoe could be bad for you"In terms of arch support and joint support, it's not the best style, but people are investing a bit more, getting their flip-flops customised, because it's something that is just so easy to wear," Baidoo says.Podiatrist Dr Helen Branthwaite, who is also chief clinical adviser at the Royal College of Podiatry, says it's "not accurate" to say flip-flops are bad.The problem comes if you go straight from wearing a very structured shoe to wearing flip-flops a lot, she explains. It means your foot is under more strain than normal, which makes you more prone to injury."The foot does start to change shape and tends to splay a little bit over time," says Branthwaite."A good analogy is if you were to wear a corset all the time and then took the corset off, everything would sort of all hang out, so to speak."So what are the stylish and comfortable alternatives?How to find healthy sandalsBaidoo suggests a more supportive flip-flop, such as a FitFlop, which is sturdier and contoured - a world away from the flat and thin flip-flops that have been cut from a big sheet of foam.Sliders are out and Crocs are in for Gen Z, she says. They might be "anti-fashion shoes" but they're "really comfy" and designed "orthopaedically" with footbed sandals like Birkenstocks offering the same advantages.The wooden clog is also making a comeback. It's worn by doctors and chefs on their feet all day. Scholl slider mules are the original orthopaedic shoe, Baidoo says - and admits she once had a pair in pink suede.Wedges are another option in the heat. "When I speak to some of my friends and some of my clients who work in the plus-size category, the wedge actually provides a form of comfortable footwear. And it provides a nice kind of silhouette for the ankle. You've got the support all the way through the shoe."Image source, Getty ImagesYou could always opt for the fisherman-style sandal, which looks like something a history teacher might have worn in the 1970s. With socks."Men can wear it as an alternative to a loafer. It's not as casual as a flip-flop, which might not be suitable for certain environments. It's a really cool kind of style to adopt for women too," Baidoo says.So what about the trend for wearing minimalist barefoot shoes? It's all about easing into them, says Branthwaite. In other words, don't buy a pair and then decide to go on a 5-mile hike.Expert tips for happy feet Podiatrist Dr Helen Branthwaite's top tips for looking after your feet: Pay close attention to the sole of the shoe and what it's made from, because that will influence how your foot moves and how you walkIf you can bend your flip-flops in two, then ask yourself if you're strong enough to take on the extra load your normal shoe would supportDon't forget to check the condition of your feet - the skin can dry out quickly in open footwear like flip-flops. You might not notice until your heel gets firmer and your toenails start to look fragileLather your feet in emollient, a moisturising water retention cream containing urea to hydrate the skin, every dayYour feet change constantly throughout your life, so get them measured regularly. Just because you start out being a size 6, doesn't mean you'll remain a size 6.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: From flip flops to fisherman's sandals: How to look after your feet this summer
